title: COMP/MCCAA/13/2025 – Assessment of the Acquisition of Sole Control by BT Group Limited of M.A.&A. Services Limited (Phase I Decision)
text:
Assessment of the Acquisition of Sole Control by BT Group Limited of M.A.&A. Services
Limited
(Phase I Decision)
Office for Competition - Case COMP/MCCAA/13/2025
12 August 2025
Decision on Proposed Acquisition in terms of Regulations 6(1)(ii) of the Control of
Concentrations Regulations (LN 294 of 2002 as subsequently amended)
NON-CONFIDENTIAL VERSION
In accordance with Article 28 of the Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority Act, any
information which the Office for Competition considered to be confidential and/or revealing business
secrets has been redacted from this version. All omissions are indicated by [✄]. Not all omissions
necessarily constitute confidential data.
Done at the Office for Competition, Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority, Mizzi House,
National Road, Blata l-Bajda, Malta on 12th August 2025.

Members of the Office for Competition who conducted the Assessment of this concentration
Dr Melchior Vella (Director, Primary Manufacturing and Retail Markets)
Sean Buttigieg (Senior Economics Manager)
Timothy Farrugia (Senior Professional Officer (Economics))
The Office for Competition would also like to thank Denise Camilleri (Director) for the valuable
contributions.
Office for Competition - 2 -

1 SUMMARY
1. On Monday 30 June 2025, the Office for Competition (hereinafter referred to as “the Office”)
within the Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority received notification of a proposed
concentration pursuant to Article 6 of the Control of Concentrations Regulations (Subsidiary
Legislation 379.08) between BT Group Limited (Birkirkara) and M.A.&A. Services Limited (Ħal
Qormi).
2. The nature of the concentration is the acquisition of sole control by BT Group Limited of M.A.&A.
Services Limited.
3. BT Group Limited fully owns BT Commercial Limited, which imports products in the field of air
heating and cooling, water heating, ventilation, air quality, and environmentally friendly energy
solutions from renowned brands, in particular “Gree”.
4. M.A.&A. Services Limited is engaged in the supply, installation, and servicing of VRF Air-
Conditioning Systems, Ventilation, Chilled Water Systems, HVAC Systems, and Building
Management Systems, amongst others, as well as the provision of all ancillary services related
thereto, in particular representing the brand “Daikin” in Malta.
5. After a detailed competitive assessment of the proposed concentration, the Office concludes
that the concentration will not lead to a substantial lessening of competition (hereinafter referred
to as “SLC”) in the affected markets, since the involved parties will continue to face strong
competition.
2 THE PARTIES
6. BT Group Limited (hereinafter referred to as “BT” or “the Notifying Party”) having company
registration number C101263 is a limited liability company registered under the laws of Malta.
Its registered office is at The Watercourse, Zone 2, Central Business District. Triq l-Imdina,
Birkirkara, CBD 2010. For the financial year, 2024, the company, through its subsidiary BT
Commercial Limited, generated a total turnover of [] in Malta.
7. BT Commercial Limited (hereinafter referred to as “BTC”) having company registration number
C25151 is a limited liability company registered under the laws of Malta. Its registered office is
at The Watercourse, Zone 2, Central Business District. Triq l-Imdina, Birkirkara, CBD 2010.
8. BT fully owns BTC, which imports products from renowned brands, in particular “Gree”, in the
field of air heating and cooling, water heating, ventilation, air quality, and environmentally
friendly energy solutions.
Office for Competition - 3 -

9. M.A.&A. Services Limited (hereinafter referred to as “MAA” or “the Target”) having company
registration number C31650 is a limited liability company registered under the laws of Malta. Its
registered office is at Centre House, Level 1, Triq il-Belt Valletta, Ħal Qormi, QRM 3619. For
the financial year, 2024, the Target generated a total turnover of [] in Malta.
10. MAA is engaged in the supply, installation, and servicing of VRF Air-Conditioning Systems,
Ventilation, Chilled Water Systems, HVAC Systems, and Building Management Systems,
amongst others, as well as the provision of all ancillary services related thereto, in particular
representing the brand “Daikin” in Malta.
11. BTC primarily operates as a wholesaler of residential air-conditioning units, with approximately
[] of its imported residential units sold to third-party distributors or operators. These
intermediaries then handle the retail sale, installation, and related value-added services to end-
users, typically households. Commercial sales and contracts of BTC are typically supported by
independent third-party contractors for installation, thereby limiting the degree of vertical
integration in its operations. In contrast, the Target is predominantly active in the medium-to-
heavy industrial and commercial segment, which accounts for around [] of its turnover. MAA
relies on its in-house workforce for installations but still engages third-party contractors to
support the execution of contracts and ongoing operations. This reliance on a mixed model of
internal and external resources is consistent with prevailing industry practices observed among
other operators active in commercial HVAC contracts.
12. The Notifying Party and the Target shall together be referred to as “the Parties”.
3 PROPOSED TRANSACTION
13. Pursuant to a Preliminary Binding Agreement signed on 5 May 2025, the Proposed Transaction
will result in the acquisition of the Target by the Notifying Party, hence acquiring sole control of
the Target.
14. The terms of the transactions that will take place in accordance with the final agreement, [].
15. The scope of the Proposed Transaction is fundamentally driven by a technical imperative to
unlock significant synergistic value and drive innovation across both the residential and
commercial/industrial segments, leading to optimised resource allocation and advanced
service capabilities.
16. The Proposed Transaction is conditional on the clearance by the Office, declaring the
transaction a lawful concentration in terms of the Control of Concentration Regulations.
Office for Competition - 4 -

4 PROCEDURE
17. The Office conducted meetings with the authorised representative of the Notifying Parties and
had a number of exchanges prior to the notification of concentration. The notification of
concentration was deemed complete on 1 July 2025.
18. The filing and acceptance of the concentration notification was notified to the public through a
notice that appeared in a local daily newspaper, on the Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs
Authority's website1 and a public notice that appeared in the Government Gazette (No. 21,465)2
on Tuesday, 8 July 2025.
19. In compiling the competitive assessment, the Office has relied on relevant guidelines issued by
the European Commission and on European competition case law.
20. In its assessment, the Office has also relied on three main sources of data (i) information
submitted by the Notifying Parties (ii) Requests for Information (hereinafter referred to as “RFI”)
sent to the Parties, (iii) RFIs sent to the competitors operating in the same market as the Parties,
more specifically in the wholesale supply of air-conditioning systems. Among other things, the
scope of the RFI, was for the Office to define and assess the size of the product market and
ask for views on the proposed acquisition.
4.1 Third-Party Views
21. On 9 July 2025, the Office sent RFIs to the parties’ main competitors to gather information and
any third-party objections. Most of the third parties replied with concerns that the concentration
will potentially lead to reduced competition.
22. Most of the third parties claimed that the concentration will lead to a dominant market position
for the Parties that will lead to a monopolistic environment. The parties will consolidate their
market power in both the residential and commercial markets. They would be able to exert their
strengthened influence on the market. Such an environment will lead to limited options to
consumers, thus potentially leading to a rise in price as customers will have reduced leverage
and choice.
23. One third-party respondent expressed concern that the proposed acquisition would result in a
single entity holding a dominant position in both the residential and commercial HVAC markets
in Malta. According to the respondent, BTC is the leading player in the residential segment,
1 Notification of Concentration < https://mccaa.org.mt/section/content?contentId=13271 > last accessed on 8 July 2025
2Notification of Concentration <
https://www.gov.mt/en/Government/DOI/Government%20Gazette/Documents/2025/07/Government%20Gazette%20-
%208th%20July.pdf > last accessed on 8 July 2025
Office for Competition - 5 -

while MAA leads the commercial market. The respondent argued that the transaction could
significantly reduce competition by consolidating market power under one contractor,
particularly given the strength of brands like Gree in the residential segment and Daikin in
commercial and VRF systems. It was suggested that the merged entity could potentially distort
market dynamics to the detriment of other competitors.
24. It was also objected that since the Parties to the concentration will consolidate their market
power in both residential and commercial markets, they will be able to offer a larger range of
products than their competitors, further strengthening their position in the market. In fact, four
out of eight respondents shared a concern that this concentration will create significant entry
and expansion barriers in the market. In particular, they argue that competitors will find it harder
to compete, whilst smaller companies will potentially be squeezed out of the market. One
respondent claimed that it would be hard to compete for tenders in such an environment.
25. Three respondents directly mentioned that the concentration will potentially lead to a rise in
prices for the reasons mentioned above. This is the case since one dominant player will have
the power to raise prices in the absence of competition. Choice and innovation will also be
affected as the Parties would have little incentive to improve services or adopt new
technologies. It was also claimed that vertical risks will potentially arise, such the expanded
vertical integration may make it more difficult for smaller firms to compete.
26. One respondent went into more detail, claiming that the market is mainly accounted for by nine
key players, including the parties, which it estimates to have a combined market share of []
in the HVAC market, based on revenue. Individually, BT has [] market shares, whilst MA has
[], both already being the two largest players in the market. The next two largest competitors,
which have a similar market share to each other, individually have around a quarter market
share of what the combined entity will have.
27. A third party put forward the argument that the potential for growth in the market is moderate
due to slower growth in new developments in the construction sector. Thus, there is increased
focus on replacements, retrofits and upgrades of current units. This leads to a market
saturation, which means that companies will compete to retain customers, as opposed to
competing for new clients. The merging of the two largest players in the market will make it
more difficult for the smaller players to compete.
28. Some respondents also argued that though multiple players can access internationals brands
while maintaining high standards of technical and after sales services agreements, such
agreements act as a natural barrier to entry, especially on the mid to high-value systems where
service quality is essential. However, for low-end or budget units, sourcing from non-local
Office for Competition - 6 -

suppliers remains a viable potential, although not an efficient alternative, for price-sensitive
consumers in the resident segment.
29. It was also noted that not all competitors are active in both the residential and commercial
segments. The Proposed Transaction would enable the Parties to consolidate their position
across both markets, giving them a unique competitive advantage. The merging parties enjoy
a good reputation with a well perceived brand image and a highly skilled technical and after-
sales workforce, which are both key in retaining customers. The merged entity can potentially
leverage its increased market strength abusively. Remaining market players will find it harder
to compete, whilst smaller players will be driven out of the market.
30. Finally, one respondent warned that the merger could trigger aggressive competition in pricing
and the offering of extended warranties, which could render the market unsustainable for other
competitors over the longer term.
4.2 Parties reply to the objections
31. On 4 August 2025, the Notifying Party submitted its reply to the third-party objections. BT
claimed that some objections show that the Proposed Transaction would further increase
competition, rather than substantially lessen it. This is based on third-party observations that
the Parties’ businesses were built on a foundation of quality products, supported by strong
technical expertise and customer service. It was also noted that the Parties remained
competitive through their pricing and by offering extended warranties.
32. The Notifying Party emphasised that there are more than 30 air conditioner brands on the
market, represented by more than 18 local operators, some long established. Other established
brands include, but are not limited to, Midea, Mitsubishi, AUX and LG. The Notifying Party
reiterated that BTC mainly caters for the residential sector and MAA for the commercial. It also
explained that there is a base effect for MAA’s market shares due to one-off contracts which
are not the norm.
33. The Notifying Party acknowledged that the Proposed Transaction would result in an increase
in market shares in both the residential and commercial segments. However, BTC argued that
this increase is not expected to harm competition. Instead, it may incentivise existing
competitors to strengthen their market positions and compete more. The Notifying Party
submitted that such dynamics could foster innovation and enhance competitive pressure in the
market. It was also noted that two players in the residential segment have shown steady growth
over recent years. Furthermore, in the residential segment, the anticipated increase in market
share relates only to a small increment at the import level, which does not necessarily reflect
the competitive dynamics on the sales side of the market.
Office for Competition - 7 -

34. As opposed to raising barriers to entry, according to the Notifying Party, the Proposed
Transaction mitigates them. BT’s success stems from having ample stocks and spare parts,
followed by strong after sales service. It works with multiple independent retail operators and
installers with non-binding agreements. None of them are tied to BT. This demonstrates BT’s
aversion to vertical integration. The presence of non-exclusive agreements is a benefit to the
market. Also, the parties deny that there are barriers to entry and claim that entering the market
is sufficiently easy.
35. The Notifying Party also argued that though the concentration will remove competition between
two large firms, the market is sufficiently competitive and there are a significant number of firms.
Post transaction, the parties have no incentive to raise prices as a substantial number of
customers would switch to a competitor. Moreover, as already stated, the Parties have current
strengths in different markets. Residential and commercial markets are largely distinct as
products within these markets are not easily substitutable. For example, a resident customer
does not have a need for a commercial HVAC, whilst a commercial customer has no need for
a resident HVAC.
36. Regarding tendering, the Parties claimed that the concentration will not change the current
scenario. Daikin is a high price top end brand that is not competitively priced for tenders. Also,
MAA is not an active participant in tendering.
37. The Notifying Party refutes that there is little potential for growth and claims that there is still
strong potential for it. Should there be a downturn in the economy, it will be up to the operators,
the parties included, to innovate, change and tackle the new challenge. In any market there will
be small and large players. Small companies are not necessarily at a disadvantage and can
still compete effectively. It is important to note that some companies remain small by choice as
it suits their business model.
5 RELEVANT MARKET
38. This section defines the appropriate definition of the product market for the purpose of providing
the framework for the competitive assessment of the proposed concentration.
39. The relevant product market concept implies that there can be effective competition between
the products that form part of it. In the European Commission’s notice on market definition, it is
stated that
“The relevant product market comprises all those products that customers
regard as interchangeable or substitutable to the product(s) of the
undertaking(s) involved, based on the products’ characteristics, their prices
Office for Competition - 8 -

and their intended use, taking into consideration the conditions of
competition and the structure of supply and demand on the market”.3
5.1 Product Scope
40. The relevant market concept implies that there can be effective competition between the
products that form part of it. In the European Commission’s notice on market definition, it is
stated that
“a relevant product market comprises all those products and/or services
which are regarded as interchangeable or substitutable by the consumer,
by reason of the products’ characteristics, their prices and their intended
use”. 4
41. HVAC systems are, in essence, air-conditioning units that supply conditioned air to buildings,
that is, air that has been modified in temperature to reach a comfortable indoor climate. These
systems use different technologies and are available in a wide range of sizes and designs to
match various building types and scales.
42. HVAC systems can be broadly categorised according to their design and intended use.
Common types include central air conditioning systems (which may incorporate components
such as Air Handling Units or use Variable Refrigerant Flow technology), chillers (typically used
in commercial and industrial settings), packaged air conditioning systems (with all key
components housed in a single outdoor unit), and split air conditioning systems (featuring
separate indoor and outdoor units). The choice of system generally depends on the
specifications of the building and functional requirements of the end-user. HVAC systems are
distributed either directly by manufacturers or indirectly via third-party distributors, resellers,
system integrators, or specialised HVAC installers.
5.1.1 Views of the Parties
43. The Notifying Party submits that the economic sectors involved in the proposed concentration
are as follows: the importation of air-conditioning systems for domestic/residential purposes;
the importation of air-conditioning systems for commercial purposes; the sale of air-conditioning
systems for domestic/residential purposes directly to end-users; the sale of air-conditioning
systems for domestic/residential proposes to intermediaries, qua installers; the sale of air-
conditioning systems for commercial purposes; the servicing and maintenance of air-
conditioning systems for domestic purposes; and the servicing and maintenance of air-
conditioning systems for commercial purposes.
3 Commission Notice on the definition of the relevant market for the purposes of Union competition law (C/2024/1645), para 12.
4 Commission Notice on the definition of the relevant market for the purposes of Union competition law (C/2024/1645), para 6.
Office for Competition - 9 -

44. The Notifying Party explains that residential and small commercial air-conditioning systems are
typically used in households and small businesses and are generally considered standardised,
commoditised products. Medium commercial systems are designed for use in places like small
offices, hotels, and shopping centres. In contrast, large commercial and industrial systems are
intended for large offices, hotels, public buildings, and industrial facilities. In the medium and
large segments, the products are often tailored to specific needs, with service and after-sales
support playing a crucial role.
45. The Notifying Party also notes that tenders and commercial installations business-to-business
(B2B) are awarded through a highly competitive negotiation process that extends beyond
pricing alone. Well-established suppliers representing a range of internationally recognised
brands compete aggressively to secure contracts, often leveraging service quality, technical
support, and product availability in addition to price.
46. The Notifying Party opines that the market in this case should be defined using the more
detailed approach, distinguishing between (i) residential and light commercial air-conditioning
systems, (ii) medium industrial and commercial systems, and (iii) large or heavy industrial and
commercial systems. Alternatively, a broader distinction between residential and commercial
air-conditioning systems would also suffice. These categories are fundamentally separate in
terms of customer types and the nature of the equipment supplied.
5.1.2 Previous approach of the Office for Competition
47. In COMP/MCCAA/01/2022 (Carrier/Toshiba Carrier), the Office described HVAC as
technologies used to control air temperature, humidity, and purity in enclosed spaces, primarily
through air-conditioning systems.5 The Office considered that the relevant product markets
included HVAC systems for buildings, with a distinction made between residential and
light/small commercial systems and medium commercial systems, in line with the areas of
activity of the parties to that transaction.
5.1.3 Previous approach of the European Commission and other National Competition Authorities
48. The European Commission has examined the HVAC sector in various past cases.6 In doing so,
it assessed whether the sector should be segmented into distinct product markets based on
5 COMP/MCCAA/01/2022 (Carrier/Toshiba Carrier), available at https://mccaa.org.mt/media/7433/acquisition-of-sole-control-
over-toshiba-carrier-corporation-by-carrier-corporation_non-confidential.pdf
6 See for example, Case No COMP/M.7375 - UTC / CIAT, available at:
https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m7375_20141205_20310_4068378_EN.pdf; Case No
Office for Competition - 10 -

factors such as cooling capacity, technology, and type of product. Nonetheless, in each of these
concentration decisions, the European Commission ultimately did not reach a definitive
conclusion on the exact scope of the product market, and consequently, left it open.
49. The Irish Competition and Consumer Protection Commission has previously assessed
transactions involving the HVAC sector without reaching a definitive conclusion on product
market definition. In one case, the Commission considered whether distinctions between
different HVAC system types were necessary but ultimately left the market definition open,
focusing instead on the competitive effects in the supply, installation, and maintenance of
HVAC systems within the State.7 In another case, the Commission also left the relevant product
markets open, as it would not alter the outcome of the competitive assessment.8 For analytical
purposes, the transaction was evaluated in relation to two potential product markets: (i) the
wholesale supply and distribution of HVAC equipment; and (ii) the supply, installation, and
maintenance of HVAC systems.
50. The Italian Competition Authority has previously distinguished between different segments
within the air-conditioning sector when defining product markets.9 In particular, it differentiated
between systems for residential, commercial, and industrial use. Residential systems were
considered distinct due to their simpler installation, lower maintenance needs, and retail-based
distribution. Commercial and industrial systems, while also distinct from one another in terms
of size, capacity, and pricing, were both characterised by advanced technology, specialised
installation, and more complex distribution channels. Such distinctions were informed by
differences in technical specifications, installation requirements, and distribution structures
across customer segments.
5.1.4 Views of the Office for Competition
51. The Office finds no justification to deviate from the approach taken in COMP/MCCAA/01/2022
(Carrier/Toshiba Carrier). In the present case, it is not necessary to determine the precise
boundaries of the relevant product markets, as this would not affect the analysis of the
competitive impact of the Proposed Transaction, and consequently, it leaves the product
market definition open.
COMP/M.5421 – PANASONIC / SANYO, available at:
https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m5421_20090929_20212_en.pdf; Case No COMP/M.4271 - DAIKIN
/ OYL, available at: https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m4271_20061002_20310_en.pdf; and Case No
IV/M.1433 – CARRIER CORPORATION / TOSHIBA, available at:
https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m1433_en.pdf.
7 Case M/21/048 – Tyco International/Airflow, available at: https://www.ccpc.ie/business/wp-
content/uploads/sites/3/2021/09/2022.01.25-M.21.048-DET-Public.pdf
8 Case M/25/006 – Mitsubishi Electric Europe / Crystal Air Holdings Limited, available at: https://www.ccpc.ie/business/wp-
content/uploads/sites/3/2025/01/M.25.006-Public-Determination.pdf
9 C5233 – Daikin Investments Italy / Siti.
Office for Competition - 11 -

52. The Office observes that air-conditioning systems vary significantly across residential,
commercial and industrial segments. Residential systems are characterised by their simplicity,
requiring minimal maintenance and only limited technical expertise for installation. These
systems are typically sold through retail outlets and independent distributors. In contrast,
commercial and industrial air-conditioning systems are more complex and tailored to larger
spaces such as offices, hotels, shopping centres, and industrial facilities. They rely on
advanced technologies to ensure higher performance, particularly in terms of safety, cooling
capacity, and energy efficiency. Commercial systems differ from industrial ones in size, power,
price, and customer requirements. Furthermore, the provision of installation and after-sales
services for commercial and industrial systems is more specialised, often involving direct sales
by manufacturers or could involve exclusive distribution contracts or long-term contracts.
Distribution channels also differ; commercial systems are usually supplied to specialised
installers via manufacturers or national wholesalers, while industrial systems are sold through
direct engagements between producers and large corporate clients or via construction firms
and thermo-technical consultants who advise on system specifications and oversee installation.
53. While the Office has left the relevant product market definition open, it has assessed whether
the Proposed Transaction may result in a SLC by analysing its potential impact on the overall
market for:
a. the supply, installation and maintenance of air-conditioning systems for residential use,
and
b. the supply, installation and maintenance of air-conditioning systems for commercial and
industrial use.
5.2 Geographic Market
54. The Office has also considered the relevant geographic market definition, which set out the
area within which it assessed the concentration.
55. The European Commission defines the relevant geographic market as
“comprises the geographic area in which the undertakings involved supply
or demand relevant products, in which the conditions of competition are
sufficiently homogeneous for the effects of the conduct or concentration
under investigation to be able to be assessed, and which can be
distinguished from other geographic areas, in particular because
conditions of competition are appreciably different in those areas”.10
10 Commission Notice on the definition of the relevant market for the purposes of Community competition law (C/2024/1645),
para 12.
Office for Competition - 12 -

5.2.1 Views of the Parties
56. The Notifying Party is of the opinion that the relevant geographic market in this case is likely to
be EEA wide in most cases, as there is some evidence that following a small but significant
increase in prices, independent distributors have sourced air conditioning systems from EEA
states, most notably from Sicily. However, it is possible for the geographic market to be left
open, as even considering a national geographic market, there will be no significant impact on
competition following the proposed transaction.
5.2.2 Previous approach of the Office for Competition
57. In COMP/MCCAA/01/2022 (Carrier/Toshiba Carrier), it was considered that, since the Parties
involved sell products in the relevant markets to independent distributors, who then resell these
products to end consumers in Malta, the relevant geographic market is predominantly national
in scope.11
5.2.3 Previous approach of the European Commission and other National Competition Authorities
58. In case M.7375 – UTC / CIAT, the European Commission argued that the geographic scope of
the HVAC systems market could extend beyond national boundaries, although some evidence
pointed to a national-level market. Ultimately, the Commission did not find it necessary to define
the geographic market precisely in that instance.12
59. Similarly, in case M.5421 – PANASONIC / SANYO, the market investigation yielded
inconclusive results regarding whether the relevant geographic market was national or broader.
As a result, the Commission left the geographic market definition open.13
60. In case M.4271 – DAIKIN / OYL, the Commission acknowledged that while HVAC products
tend to be relatively uniform across Europe, certain market characteristics vary between EEA
countries. Consequently, the Commission also chose not to establish a definitive geographic
market definition in that case.14
61. In M/21/048 - Tyco International/Airflow15 and M/25/006 – Mitsubishi Electric Europe / Crystal
Air Holdings Limited16, the Irish Competition and Consumer Protection Commission ultimately

carrier-corporation-by-carrier-corporation_non-confidential.pdf
12 Case No COMP/M.7375 - UTC / CIAT, para. 26., available at:
https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m7375_20141205_20310_4068378_EN.pdf
13 Case No COMP/M.5421 - PANASONIC / SANYO, paras. 25-27., available at:
https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m5421_20090929_20212_en.pdf

https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m4271_20061002_20310_en.pdf
15 Case M/21/048 – Tyco International/Airflow, available at: https://www.ccpc.ie/business/wp-
content/uploads/sites/3/2021/09/2022.01.25-M.21.048-DET-Public.pdf
16 Case M/25/006 – Mitsubishi Electric Europe / Crystal Air Holdings Limited, available at: https://www.ccpc.ie/business/wp-
content/uploads/sites/3/2025/01/M.25.006-Public-Determination.pdf
Office for Competition - 13 -

left the geographic market definition open but analysed the impact of that transaction by
reference to the State.
62. The Italian Competition Authority considered that the scope of the geographic market was at
least national, taking into account: (a) that customers are based in the national territory; (b) that
price conditions are applied at a national level; and (c) that distribution is carried out through
resellers that are active at a national level.17
5.2.4 Views of the Office for Competition
63. In delineating the geographic market, it is considered that the scope is at least national. This
reflects the fact that customers are located within the national territory, pricing practices are
applied uniformly across the country, and distribution is carried out through resellers operating
nationally. However, in this instance, it is not necessary to define the geographic market with
precision, as the competitive assessment of the Proposed Transaction remains unchanged
regardless of the exact scope. For the purposes of this analysis, the likely competitive effects
have been assessed at the national level.
6 INDUSTRY BACKGROUND
6.1 Trends in the use of air-conditioning systems
64. In terms of demand, the Office notes that according to the NSO’s Census of Population and
Housing 2021 Final Report on Dwelling Characteristics, air-conditioning systems were present
in at least 80% of all primary residences, with a broadly consistent distribution across the six
districts.18 This represents a significant rise from 52.1% in 2011 and 45.3% in 2005, indicating
a steady increase in adoption over time. The highest rates of air-conditioner ownership were
recorded in localities such as Swieqi (91.3%), Ħ’Attard (90.3%), Iklin (89.8%), and Naxxar
(88%), while the lowest were observed in Mdina (57.3%), Valletta (74.2%), and Isla (74.9%).
65. In Malta, air-conditioning accounts for a significantly higher share of household electricity
consumption compared to the EU average. While air-conditioning represented just 2.5% of total
household electricity use across the EU in 2022, the share in Malta is considerably greater,
ranging between 8% and 25%. This reflects the penetration of air-conditioning units and their
increasing use. Furthermore, Malta’s elevated share of average per-dwelling electricity
consumption for air-conditioning highlights the increasing importance of this end-use in the local

Statistics Office. Available at: https://nso.gov.mt/wp-content/uploads/Census-2021-Volume-2.pdf (Accessed: 7 July 2025).
Office for Competition - 14 -

energy profile. The consumption per dwelling for air-conditioning increased from 373kWh in
2010 to 928 kWh per dwelling in 2022.19
Figure 1: Consumption per dwelling for air-conditioning
Source: Odyssee-Mure

7.1 Horizontal Effects
7.1.1 Analytical framework
71. The Commission Guidelines on the assessment of horizontal mergers under the Council
Regulation on the control of concentrations between undertakings (the “Horizontal Merger
Guidelines”)20 distinguish between two main ways in which mergers between actual or
potential competitors on the same relevant market may significantly impede effective
competition, namely non-coordinated and coordinated effects.
72. Coordinated effects may significantly impede effective competition by changing the nature of
competition in such a way that firms that previously were not coordinating their behaviour, are
now significantly more likely to coordinate and raise prices or otherwise harm effective
competition. A merger may also make coordination easier, more stable or more effective for
firms which were coordinating prior to the merger.
73. Coordination may take various forms. In some markets, the most likely coordination may
involve keeping prices above the competitive level. In other markets, coordination may aim at
limiting production or the amount of new capacity brought to the market.
74. Non-coordinated effects may significantly impede effective competition by eliminating important
competitive constraints on one or more firms, which consequently would have increased market
power, without resorting to coordinated behaviour. In that regard, the Horizontal Merger
Guidelines consider not only the direct loss of competition between the merging firms, but also
the reduction in competitive pressure on non-merging firms in the same market that could be
brought about by the merger.21
75. The Horizontal Merger Guidelines list a number of factors, which may influence the rise of
substantial non-coordinated, effects from a merger, such as: the large market shares of the
merging firms; the fact that the merging firms are close competitors; the limited possibilities for
customers to switch suppliers; or the fact that the merger would eliminate an important
competitive force. That list of factors applies equally if a merger would create or strengthen a

7.2 Coordinated Effects
107. As noted above, coordinated effects may arise when a Proposed Transaction alters competitive
dynamics in a way that makes it more likely for the merged entity and other market players to
align their behaviour – for example, by increasing prices or reducing output. The central issue
is whether the transaction would significantly raise the probability of successful coordination
among firms or reinforce any existing coordinated practices in the market.25

108. Based on the information in the Office’s possession, the likely effects of the Proposed
Transaction are mainly unilateral in nature. The Proposed Transaction, in itself, has not
presented a plausible coordinated effects theory of harm.
109. On the basis of the information in the possession of the Office, no plausible coordinated effects
theory of harm was identified given the relevant counterfactual. Therefore, no further discussion

7.3 Vertical Effects
110. As noted above, BTC operates primarily as a wholesale supplier of air-conditioning units,
particularly in the residential segment, and does not engage in downstream activities such as
installation or direct sales to end-users. These functions are carried out by independent third-
party contractors, operating on their own account. Although MAA is active in the commercial
segment and undertakes some installation work through its internal workforce, it remains reliant
on third-party contractors to fulfil and support its contracts. This reliance on external service
providers is common across the industry and reflects a market structure with limited vertical
integration.
111. The Office considers that the Proposed Transaction does not result in BTC gaining the ability
or incentive to engage in input foreclosure. First, there will remain a range of air-conditioning
equipment suppliers and distributors following implementation of the Proposed Transaction.
The Office notes that there are several undertakings in the wholesale supply and distribution of
air-conditioning equipment, and that that distributors will continue to be able to source air-
conditioning equipment from these importers following implementation of the Proposed
Transaction. Therefore, the Office considers that BTC will not have the ability to engage in input
foreclosure post-Proposed Transaction. Second, BTC mainly acts as a wholesale supplier of
air-conditioning units, especially for the residential segment. Installation services are handled
by independent third-party contractors. Although MAA performs some installation work in the
commercial segment using its own personnel, it still relies on third-party contractors to support
its operations. This indicates that its level of vertical integration remains limited.
112. Given the nature of the Parties’ operations, the concentration does not give rise to vertical
effects concerns. Accordingly, the Proposed Transaction is not expected to result in input or
customer foreclosure, or to raise barriers to entry or expansion for competing downstream
operators.
